I recently read 'The Book of Love' after being such a good book the first time I read it. I am afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. One of the things that I did not like was way that John Fenton was portrayed. It was not necessary to see him as a young and selfish man. The movie changed the relationship between James Fenton and his wife quite a lot and made their sexual relationship seem too much. Also, there was much less of a connection between Charles Fenton and the detective than was originally portrayed in the book. The movie sent the two in almost completely opposite ways and it did not seem to develop their relationship. Instead, it felt like they happened to be together in the story. A fine movie, but I think that it really could have been better than it was, had it more closely stayed true to the book.

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a drunken Swedish book editor who finds himself on a train from Stockholm to Berlin. According to everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. There's also a wealthy man and his mistress, a woman trying to escape her husband (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, a group of gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two gangsters, a group of refugees, and even a journalist. Meant to combine elements of noir, thriller (which it does quite well, at least to begin with), and comedy, the film struggles with consistency. It doesn't sit well when the film changes tone with every new scene, and as the train heads towards its final destination, the film seems to lose its altogether, ending on a rather surreal note. A good cast is wasted on a myriad of different plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with talented Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the director gathered everyone he's ever worked with and gave them a part in the film. Of course, the actors are only as good as the script they're working with - don't blame them. The comedy is often forced and unfunny, and the thriller elements are over the top. The pacing is painfully slow at times (quite a few times), with one scene in particular dragging on for over ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to resort to swearing and other profanity to avoid decent dialogue. The film looks good though, in all honesty. There's a lot of wasted potential, but the film fails in every other department. 3/10

I, like many other people, saw this movie after years of not trying to find it. Oddly enough, it was easier to find than I thought it would be. I guess it shouldn't come as a surprise that I found it used. It can be summed up quite masterfully in the title itself: A possessed bed eats people. Nothing more, nothing less. There is an attempt to put in a story line but not a very good one. Basically, a demon's head is thrown from a window and lands on a bed, which becomes possessed. It devours anyone that happens upon it by absorbing them then dissolving them into what appears to be orange Fanta. There is a boy who fell on to the bed when he was sick and ends up in a painting of the room it inhabits. The story is told entirely in English. This movie fails horribly at everything, even at being bad. Still, it's entertaining in its own way.

Trite and over executed. It's like someone took Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them up together, using the music and and some of the plot of those two movies to make another one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some facts that have been manipulated to better suit the story. This is true for the most part. For example, during the early part of Beethoven's life, it was common for deaf people to write down what they needed to say in order for others to understand them. This, of course, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, while filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the essence of that time. This, coupled with the bad acting, seems rather distracting. Gary Oldman is talented enough, but I hope he still has time to work on his craft. If you're really looking for information about Beethoven, don't blame Gary Oldman for it. Instead, read a biography or one of the many documentaries made about him. Or just lose yourself in the beauty of Beethoven's music. http://iwascalledclementine.blogspot.com/

This rather silly romantic comedy is based on the kind of story that, as a teenager, I always found rather distasteful. In the case of adult-teen relationships, the motivation is on the part of the elder is usually either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both, while the younger is most likely looking for the kind of attention he (or she) lacked as a child. Such hidden agendas seem more sinister than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit tired--as well he could be--as the hero of this rather silly story. He was, at least, attempting the role of a thirty-five-year-old man romancing a seventeen-year-old. But Audrey Hepburn was a revelation--pretty, lively, and full of charm--as the heroine, the seventeen-year-old presented as a gift to "The Professor," the morally upright and honest screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her excellent performance wrung from Powell a bit more than the film would otherwise deserve. Deborah Kerr was good as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and handled her small part deftly. There's some rather good dialogue in the film, too, so it's not a complete washout. 5/10

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn appears in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The script is all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one scene to the next - you are just not given the minimum information needed to keep some continuity and understand his present situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motives behind some of their behaviour. Add to that a series of silly and implausible situations and you have film that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, disjointed and totally unrealistic. There are many long, boring musical sections of the film that to me are either bad direction or a bad director trying and failing to be artistic. None of the characters are even likable and the Flynn character comes across as a self serving liar, thug, thief, robber, murderer, bear fist fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to further his own dreams, and somehow, despite all that, great opportunities just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining nor satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so why even watch it? To rub salt into the wound, the DVD had one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1, it had terrible telecine wobble and many, many artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust and scratches somewhere.

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn appears in this film, but as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The plot jumps all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one place to the next - you are often not given the background information needed to keep some continuity and understand his present situation, and it is hard to understand Flynn's and other characters' motivations and some of their behaviour, which never seem to make a modicum of sense in the situations they do have. It comes across like one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up, and try to remember it, it is all strange, disjointed and completely unrealistic. There are several long, boring musical sections of the film which to me are either poor direction or a result of the story failing to be engaging. None of the characters are interesting or even likable, and Flynn himself comes across as a self-serving, manipulative, gambler, thief, robber, murderer, bear pit fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to further his own interests, and yet, despite all that, great fortunes just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining or satisfying in any way and by all accounts is not historically accurate, so why even bother? And to rub salt in the wound, the DVD was one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide screen or Dolby 5.1, and there had been screen errors, and many, many artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust and scratches.

Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of old classic horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are occasional shots to an audience watching these films. Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen play two audience members who talk to the camera and explain why they love these films. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie horror makes us afraid of real horror", "we are at the mercy of the filmmaker in the theatre") and pretty clichéd. All the films are shown very quickly and the editing is kind of jarring. Also, shown out of context, the films aren't very scary at all. The film is also short. I saw this in the theater back in 1984 and was annoyed that I paid $7.50 for an hour and a half film! Still, it's a well made film and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. So if you have an interest in the history of terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored and think it's a bad movie (nopun intended). I give it a C.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but it unfortunately does the opposite of just that. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in his scenes in his usual attire, which he trades in for a more gentleman-like garb to meet with his love interest, Miss Rylott (Lynne Roberts). It's clear, though, why Rylott would have wanted his daughter to meet Holmes. If as is the case with Helen (played by Lynne Roberts), he didn't want her to run off to Sherlock Holmes, he would have accomplished the same thing by having Holmes leave. One of the curiosities is Holmes' interest in setting an appointment to meet with Helen, after which point he is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The inclusion of a group of people trying to solve the mystery of Colonel Stoner's death is merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting plot tool, a deadly snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a significant factor in the snake's death, the Indian asp, notwithstanding. The brief appearance of Nigel Bruce as Holmes' partner John Watson does provide the picture with some color, even if Nigel Bruce's performance is not his best. As Professor Moriarty, John Harding is appropriately menacing, a trait that should be expected given that he played Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two other films, 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Hound at the Baskervilles." With a mostly unknown cast and an unsteady director, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is still maintained, even if it stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I suppose that would be the case even with the snake's introduction, as one of the best cuts in the picture proved to be the one bringing in the asp.

Though a fan of horror and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The makeup and puppet effects were good, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but the pacing was terrible. Firstly, the first act of the movie is spent on exposition of Jack Brooks' backstory, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his past is revealed within minutes of the opening title sequence. Additionally, the narration and some of the flashbacks were needless. The majority of the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then sleeping, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the third act is mostly focused on the antics of Jack Brooks and his problems with his girlfriend. (Definitely an entertaining moment in the film, excellent and worth a few laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack gets to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: The New Nightmare had loads of potential but was poorly paced and drags on too long without adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell and Jack vs. Ash go into production.

This anime is based on the video game Street Fighter II: Zero! It takes place in an anime setting! Just like the animated movie! This movie is all about Ryu who is accompanied by Ken (who is not even recognized as a character) and Birdie! None of the other characters are used from the video game (that I could discover)! The fighting scenes were OK but nothing too special! And there were not many fighting scenes! To me this is odd! An anime should have more fighting scenes! And the animated movie (2001) is far superior to this anime! It tries to be more than it really is! The use of the "Hada Power" and other story elemnents have nothing to do with the meaning they have in the video game! And in an anime that is a big problem! The pacing is so slow that you can't even tell what is happening! The action is toned down! But why? And what happened to the other characters from the video game! Surely they are more interesting than the villain in this story! The other characters of the video game are unique fighters with their own special skills! In this movie it is all about Ryu! So, why this anime?
